questions.stem: A patient is diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes at age 10. Their pancreas produces little to no insulin. What is the most appropriate long-term treatment?

options.text: A controlled diet and regular exercise alone
Regular insulin injections to replace the insulin their pancreas cannot produce
Glucagon injections to lower blood sugar
Surgical removal of the pancreas

questions.explanation: Type 1 diabetes is caused by the immune system destroying the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. Since the body cannot make insulin, it must be replaced by regular insulin injections (or an insulin pump) to control blood glucose levels. Diet alone cannot manage Type 1 diabetes.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old patient is diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes. Their pancreas still produces insulin, but their body cells do not respond to it effectively. What is this phenomenon called?

options.text: Insulin overproduction
Insulin resistance — body cells have reduced sensitivity to insulin
Insulin allergy
Glucagon deficiency

questions.explanation: In Type 2 diabetes, body cells become resistant to insulin — their receptors no longer respond effectively to the hormone. Even though insulin is produced, cells do not take up glucose from the blood properly, leading to high blood glucose levels. This is often linked to obesity and lifestyle factors.

questions.stem: A person with diabetes injects too much insulin by mistake. What dangerous condition could this cause, and what are the symptoms?

options.text: Hyperglycaemia — too much glucose in the blood, causing frequent urination
Hypoglycaemia — blood glucose drops too low, causing shakiness, confusion, and potentially unconsciousness
Dehydration — all water is lost from the blood
Hyperglycaemia — glucose accumulates in the liver

questions.explanation: Too much insulin causes cells to absorb too much glucose from the blood, leading to hypoglycaemia (dangerously low blood glucose). The brain depends on glucose for energy, so symptoms include shakiness, confusion, dizziness, and if severe, loss of consciousness or seizures.

questions.stem: The rate of Type 2 diabetes is increasing globally. Which factor is most strongly linked to this increase?

options.text: Increased use of antibiotics
Rising obesity rates due to high-sugar diets and sedentary lifestyles
Increased exposure to viruses that attack the pancreas
Genetic mutations caused by air pollution

questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes is strongly linked to obesity, poor diet (high in sugar and processed foods), and lack of exercise. As these lifestyle factors become more common worldwide, the prevalence of Type 2 diabetes increases. It is a major global health concern.

questions.stem: A doctor recommends that a Type 2 diabetes patient manages their condition through diet and exercise before considering medication. Why might regular exercise help control their blood glucose?

options.text: Exercise causes the pancreas to produce more glucagon
Exercise increases the rate of glucose uptake by muscle cells for respiration and can improve insulin sensitivity
Exercise converts all blood glucose permanently into glycogen
Exercise destroys excess glucose molecules in the blood

questions.explanation: During exercise, muscles use glucose for respiration at a higher rate, directly lowering blood glucose. Regular exercise also improves insulin sensitivity — cells become more responsive to insulin, taking up glucose more effectively. Combined with a controlled diet, this can manage mild Type 2 diabetes.
